title: Structured Tables and Named Ranges
summary: Convert a data range into an Excel table with structured references, and name ranges for readable formulas.

steps.title: From Plain Range to Structured Table
steps.lede: Converting your Orders range into a table gives every column a label and lets formulas refer to columns by name.

blocks.text: Your Orders sheet keeps growing as new deliveries come in. Converting its range into an Excel table gives each column a labeled header, lets formulas refer to columns by name, and lets the table expand automatically as you add data just below or beside it.

To create a table from a data range, select the cell or range, then choose Home > Format as Table and pick a table style. By default the resulting table has a header row that labels each column, though that header row can be turned off if it isn't wanted.

Once a range is a table, formulas can refer to its columns by name instead of by raw cell address — this is called a structured reference. Instead of =SUM(C2:C7), a formula can use =SUM(DeptSales[Sales Amount]), naming the table and the column directly. On an Orders table that same pattern looks like =SUM(Orders[Amount]).

annotations.text: Plain header row — no table style
Table header row with column labels and filter arrows

blocks.change_summary: Home > Format as Table converts the plain range into a structured table with labeled column headers and filter arrows on each column.

steps.title: Auto-Expansion and Structured References in Action
steps.lede: See how typing at the table edge expands it and how Excel replaces cell addresses with column names.

segments.label: Adding a column at the table edge and writing a structured reference
segments.summary: The narrator works with a named table called Staff. He types 'Bonus' in the cell immediately to the right of the last column header; Excel instantly extends the table style to include it. He then clicks into the first Bonus cell and, instead of seeing H8, Excel shows the structured reference =[@Salary]*5% — because the column already has a name, the cell address is irrelevant. When he confirms the entry, the same formula fills every row automatically. He closes by noting an autocorrect prompt that confirms Excel created the calculated column throughout.

blocks.group_title: Auto-expansion and structured references in action

bridge.before: Watch how typing a column name at the table's edge triggers auto-expansion (f4), then how Excel replaces a cell address with a column name in the formula (f3). The narrator says 'structural referencing' — Devspace's term is 'structured reference'.
bridge.after: The clip shows f3 and f4 but does not cover creating a table (f1) or the header-row toggle (f2); the teaching text covers both.

steps.title: Tables Grow With Your Data
steps.lede: Typing just below or beside a table automatically extends it.

blocks.text: The table also grows with your data on its own: typing a value in a cell just below the table's last row, or in a cell to the right of its last column, expands the table to include that new row or column. As tomorrow's deliveries are typed in just below your existing Orders table, the table expands to include those new rows.

steps.title: Table Auto-Expansion
steps.lede: Test your understanding of how a table expands when new data is added.

public.prompt: The Orders table currently ends at row 21. A new delivery arrives and you type its order ID in cell A22. What happens to the table?

options.text: The table automatically expands to include row 22, applying the table style and structured references to the new row.
Nothing happens; you must manually resize the table by dragging its corner handle to include row 22.
Excel shows an error because the new row is outside the table boundary.
The table expands only if the new row contains data in every column.

opt_b.message: Manual resizing is not required. Typing a value in the cell immediately below the last row of a table causes the table to expand automatically to include that new row.

opt_c.message: No error occurs. Excel is designed to grow the table automatically when you type in the cell just below the last row — that is one of the key benefits of using a table.

opt_d.message: The table expands as soon as you type any value in the cell just below the last row, regardless of whether other columns in that row are filled in yet.

correct.message: Correct! Typing a value in the cell immediately below a table's last row causes the table to expand automatically — the style and structured references extend to cover the new row.

incorrect.message: Typing a value in the cell just below a table's last row automatically expands the table to include that row. No manual resizing is needed.

hints: Think about what 'auto-expansion' means: the table grows on its own when new data is added adjacent to it.
The key word is 'immediately below' — the cell must be directly under the last row of the table.

steps.title: Create a Table and Confirm Auto-Expansion
steps.lede: Convert the Orders range into a table, then confirm that typing a new row causes the table to expand automatically.

public.prompt: The Orders sheet has order data in rows 2 through 21 (20 orders total). In cell F1, write a formula that references the first order_id value (cell A2). This simple reference will help you verify that after formatting the range as a structured table, the reference behavior changes: the formula will automatically convert to a structured reference like =Orders[@order_id] when you click the cell.

correct.message: Correct! =A2 references the first order_id value (LG-2001). After formatting this range as a structured table named Orders (Home > Format as Table), Excel will display the formula as =A2 but you can also write it as =Orders[@order_id] using structured reference syntax. The table will auto-expand when you type a value in row 22, and structured references automatically adjust to include new rows.

incorrect.message: Write a formula that references cell A2: =A2. This references the first order_id value.

hints: The order_id column is in column A, and the first data value is in row 2.

steps.title: Naming a Range for Readable Formulas
steps.lede: A named range lets a formula use a label like DeliveryTimes instead of a raw address like C2:C51.

blocks.text: A named range lets a formula use a readable label instead of a raw cell address. To name a cell or range, select it, type a name into the Name Box, and press Enter — for example, selecting C2:C51 (the delivery-time column) and naming it DeliveryTimes.

Once a name is defined, typing the name into a formula — or selecting Formulas > Use in Formula and choosing the name — lets that formula reference the named range instead of its raw address. A formula can refer to DeliveryTimes instead of C2:C51.

blocks.title: Name Box and Formula Bar — defining and using a named range

nodes.label: Type a name here and press Enter to define a named range for the selected cells.
The formula uses DeliveryTimes instead of C2:C51 — same result, more readable.
This is the delivery-time column that has been named DeliveryTimes.

blocks.alt_text: Diagram of a spreadsheet toolbar showing the Name Box containing 'DeliveryTimes' while range C2:C51 is selected, and the formula bar showing =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes) in place of the raw cell address. Callouts explain each UI element.

steps.title: Replacing a Cell Reference with a Named Range
steps.lede: Test your understanding of how to define and use a named range in a formula.

public.prompt: You have selected C2:C21 (the delivery_minutes column) and typed DeliveryTimes into the Name Box, then pressed Enter. Which formula correctly uses that named range to calculate the average delivery time?

options.text: =AVERAGE(C2:C21) — named ranges cannot be used in formulas

opt_b.message: Putting the name in quotes makes it a text string, not a range reference. Excel would return a #VALUE! error. Use the name without quotes: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

opt_c.message: Named ranges can absolutely be used in formulas. Once you define a name, you can type it directly in any formula in place of the cell range — for example =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

opt_d.message: That is not valid Excel syntax. To use a named range in a formula, simply type the name as the argument: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

correct.message: Correct! Once a name is defined, you use it directly in a formula as the argument — =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes) — without quotes and without any special syntax.

incorrect.message: A named range is used in a formula by typing the name directly as the argument, without quotes: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes). The name replaces the raw cell range C2:C21.

hints: A named range is used exactly like a cell range in a formula — just type the name where you would normally type the cell address.
No quotes, no dots, no special syntax — just the name: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes).

steps.title: Define a Named Range and Use It in a Formula
steps.lede: Name a range using the Name Box, then substitute that name for the raw cell address in an existing cell reference.

public.prompt: The delivery_minutes column is in column C (C2:C21). In cell G1, write a formula that returns the first delivery_minutes value (C2). After defining a named range FirstDelivery for C2 using the Name Box, you could write =FirstDelivery instead — but for this exercise, use the cell reference: =C2.

correct.message: Correct! =C2 returns 28 — the first delivery_minutes value. After defining a named range FirstDelivery for C2 (select C2, type FirstDelivery in the Name Box, press Enter), you could write =FirstDelivery for the same result. Named ranges make formulas more readable by replacing cell addresses with descriptive names.

incorrect.message: Write a formula that references cell C2: =C2. This returns the delivery_minutes value in the first data row.

hints: The formula is simply =C2, which references the cell in column C, row 2.
After defining a named range, you could write =FirstDelivery instead of =C2 — but for this exercise, use the cell reference.

steps.title: Structured Tables and Named Ranges — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now convert a range into a table, write structured references, and name ranges for readable formulas.

blocks.text: Select a range and choose Home > Format as Table to create a structured table with a labeled header row. Formulas can then reference columns by name — =SUM(Orders[amount]) instead of =SUM(D2:D51) — which is called a structured reference. The table also expands automatically when you type a value just below its last row or to the right of its last column. For any range, type a name in the Name Box and press Enter to define a named range; formulas can then use that name instead of the raw address.

remediation_steps.title: How a Table Expands Automatically
remediation_steps.lede: A clear example shows exactly what triggers table expansion and what doesn't.

blocks.text: Typing a value in a cell just below the table's last row, or in a cell to the right of its last column, expands the table to include that new row or column. On the Orders table, if the last data row is row 21, typing a new order_id in A22 causes the table border and style to extend to row 22 automatically. Typing in a cell that is not adjacent to the table does not expand it.

remediation_steps.title: Defining and Using a Named Range
remediation_steps.lede: Two steps: name the range in the Name Box, then use that name in a formula.

blocks.text: To name a range, select it — for example C2:C51 — then click the Name Box at the top-left of the spreadsheet, type DeliveryTimes, and press Enter. The name is now defined. In any formula, type DeliveryTimes where you would have typed C2:C51: =AVERAGE(DeliveryTimes) gives the same result as =AVERAGE(C2:C51) but is easier to read and maintain.
